title: Readable names and small functions
idea: Readable code lets the next engineer see intent without running it: names state meaning and units, and each small function does one job at one level of detail.
points: Name by meaning and unit: `priceInCents` beats `r`, `rideLength` beats `t`.
Replace magic numbers with named constants and boolean flags with an `enum`.
Keep functions small: one job, one level of abstraction, few parameters.
Reject bad input early with a clear exception, never a sentinel like -1.

parts.label: Return type
parts.note: A plain number, so the name must say what it measures.

parts.label: Name with unit
parts.note: Names the result, not the action. The suffix stops cents and whole units being mixed.

parts.label: Typed quantity
parts.note: `java.time.Duration` carries its unit. Callers write `Duration.ofHours(2)`, never a bare int.

parts.label: Enum, not flag
parts.note: `DayType.WEEKEND` reads clearly at the call site; a bare `true` does not.

code.title: The problem
code.caption: Short names, a boolean flag and magic numbers hide a unit bug in plain sight.

walk.text: `calc`, `t` and `f` hide the meaning. The comment asks what the names should answer.
The caller passes 2 meaning hours; `calc` reads minutes. Each side looks right alone.
Nested ifs mix three jobs: validation, the time price and the weekend surcharge.
60, 200 and 150 are business rules with no names. Changing one means hunting for copies.
Bad input returns -1, a price-shaped number that a careless caller could charge.

code.title: The fix
code.caption: Same rules, renamed and split: a `Duration` input, a `DayType` enum, named constants.

walk.text: `Duration.ofHours(2)` puts the unit at the call site, and `DayType` names the option.
Each business rule becomes a constant whose name states the rule and its unit.
`priceInCents` reads as a summary: check inputs, add base and extra time, apply surcharge.
A guard clause rejects a zero or negative ride with a message, never a -1.
Each helper does one step at one level of detail, small enough to check at a glance.
Bad input fails loudly here, where the caller made the mistake.

pitfalls: Vague names like `calc`, `data` or `tmp` force readers into the body; name the result.
Comments that restate code go stale; rename the variable or extract a named method instead.
Dozens of one-line methods that hop around hurt too; extract only a coherent step.

quiz.q: A teammate writes `send(order, true, false)`. What is the best readability fix?
options: Replace the booleans with enums or separately named methods
Add a comment above every call explaining the flags
Rename the parameters to flag1 and flag2
Move the flags into static fields set before the call
quiz.why: Call sites then say what they mean, like `Delivery.EXPRESS`. Comments drift, renamed parameters are invisible at the call, and static flags add hidden shared state.

takeaway: Names carry meaning and units; each function does one job.
